title: Two celebrities' opinions are not common Reformed consent against Ames and the British deputies
source_text: CXLI. Sed ad institutum meum non necesse est, ut operam ponam in eorum dictis emolliendis atque excusandis. Esto enim Joannes Dallaéus & Andreas Rivetus hac in parte aliud senserint, quam Amesius, & Theologi Britanni, quorum sententia jam exposita est; & eandem certitudinem tribuerint fiduciae quam singuli fideles habere dicuntur de remissione peccatorum suorum quae competit ipsi fidei qua debemus amplecti fidei articulos: An inde sequitur posse tribui Reformatis, quod idem communi consensu cum duobus illis viris de re proposita doceant? Et quis nescit utrumque illorum habuisse peculiares quasdam opiniones, quibus hinc & inde multi ex Reformatis sese opposuerunt? Ac etiam quare potius ex duorum illorum virorum sententia Reformatorum fidem metiri deberemus, quam ex doctrina Amesii, & Theologorum Britannorum Ecclesiae Anglicanae nomine loquentium, & ab ea ad Synodum Dordracenam deputatorum?
pass_a_gloss: But for my purpose it is not necessary that I put labor into softening and excusing their sayings. For grant that Jean Daillé and Andrew Rivet felt otherwise on this point than Ames and the British Theologians whose sentence has already been set forth; and that they attributed to the fiducia which each of the faithful is said to have concerning the remission of his sins the same certainty which belongs to the faith itself by which we ought to embrace the articles of faith: Does it thence follow that it can be attributed to the Reformed that by common consent with those two men they teach the same concerning the matter proposed? And who does not know that each of them had certain peculiar opinions to which many of the Reformed here and there opposed themselves? And also why should we rather measure the faith of the Reformers from the sentence of those two men than from the doctrine of Ames and of the British Theologians speaking in the name of the Anglican Church and deputed by it to the Synod of Dort?
pass_b_english: Even granting Daillé and Rivet differed from Ames and the British — giving own-remission fiducia the same certainty as article-faith — that does not make their view common Reformed consent.
Both men held peculiar opinions many Reformed opposed.
Why weigh Reformers by those two rather than by Ames and the Anglican deputies to Dort?
